Where it appears: Al-Fatihah — How do I learn it?
English: How do I learn it?

Where it appears: Al-Fatihah — How do I learn it?
English: Take one verse at a time, listening and repeating rather than reading. The Practice screen has all seven with a recording against each, and a repeat button. Play a line, say it with the reciter, and move on when it holds. Most people need days, not minutes.

Where it appears: Al-Fatihah — How do I learn it?
English: Until you have it, say what you know and keep going. Nobody expects a first-week Muslim to have memorised it, and the prayer you pray while learning is still your prayer.
Français: En attendant de la savoir, dites ce que vous connaissez et continuez. Personne n’attend d’un musulman de sa première semaine qu’il l’ait mémorisée, et la prière que vous faites en apprenant reste votre prière.
Español: Hasta que la tengas, di lo que sepas y sigue. Nadie espera que un musulmán de su primera semana la haya memorizado, y la oración que haces mientras aprendes sigue siendo tu oración.

Where it appears: Al-Fatihah — What am I actually saying?
English: What am I actually saying?

Where it appears: Al-Fatihah — What am I actually saying?
English: It opens by praising God as the Lord of everything and the source of mercy, then turns and speaks to Him directly: You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help. The rest is a request: guide us along the straight path. It is a prayer for guidance, said before anything else is asked for.

Where it appears: Al-Fatihah — What is Al-Fatihah?
English: What is Al-Fatihah?

Where it appears: Al-Fatihah — What is Al-Fatihah?
English: The opening chapter of the Qur’an, seven short verses. Its name means "The Opening". It is the most repeated passage in the world: every Muslim says it in every unit of every prayer, which for most people is seventeen times a day.

Where it appears: Al-Fatihah — Why does every prayer need it?
English: Why does every prayer need it?

Where it appears: Al-Fatihah — Why does every prayer need it?
English: Because without it there is no prayer. The Prophet ﷺ said that whoever does not recite Al-Fatihah in their prayer, their prayer is invalid. Of everything a new Muslim could memorise, this is the one that changes what they are able to do today.
Français: Parce que sans elle il n’y a pas de prière. Le Prophète ﷺ a dit que celui qui ne récite pas Al-Fatiha dans sa prière, sa prière est invalide. De tout ce qu’un nouveau musulman pourrait mémoriser, c’est elle qui change ce qu’il peut faire aujourd’hui.
Español: Porque sin ella no hay oración. El Profeta ﷺ dijo que quien no recita Al-Fatiha en su oración, su oración es inválida. De todo lo que un musulmán nuevo podría memorizar, esta es la que cambia lo que puede hacer hoy.

Where it appears: Asking God to choose — What can I ask about?
English: What can I ask about?

Where it appears: Asking God to choose — What can I ask about?
English: Any time except the times when prayer is held off, and about anything you genuinely have a choice in: a job, a move, a marriage, something smaller. Not about whether to do something already settled as right or wrong; there is nothing to ask about there.

Where it appears: Asking God to choose — What do I say?
English: What do I say?

Where it appears: Asking God to choose — What do I say?
English: Said after the two rakʿahs. Where it says “this matter”, name the thing you are deciding.

Where it appears: Asking God to choose — What is istikhara?
English: What is istikhara?

Where it appears: Asking God to choose — What is istikhara?
English: Two rakʿahs and a duʿa, prayed when you have a decision to make. Jabir reported that the Prophet ﷺ taught it for every matter the way he taught a surah of the Qur’an, which tells you how ordinary it was meant to be, and how often.

Where it appears: Asking God to choose — What sign should I expect?
English: What sign should I expect?

Where it appears: Asking God to choose — What sign should I expect?
English: This is the part people are told wrong. The duʿa asks God, if the thing is good for you, to bring it about and make it easy, and if it is bad for you, to turn it away and turn you away from it. It does not promise a sign, a dream or a feeling. You pray, and then you decide, and what follows is the answer.

Where it appears: Asking God to choose — What sign should I expect?
English: You still have to think, ask people who know, and weigh it up. Istikhara goes alongside that, not instead of it.

Where it appears: Asr — Face the qibla and intend
English: Stand facing the qibla, feet roughly shoulder-width apart, and intend in your heart that you are praying Asr.

Where it appears: Asr — Turn to your left
English: That is Asr complete.

Where it appears: Becoming Muslim — Know what you are saying
English: Know what you are saying

Where it appears: Becoming Muslim — Know what you are saying
English: Becoming Muslim is one sentence, said and meant. Before you say it, be clear on both halves: that worship belongs to Allah alone and nothing shares that with Him, and that Muhammad ﷺ was sent by Him to convey how.

Where it appears: Becoming Muslim — Know what you are saying
English: It has to be meant. Saying the words to please someone else, or to marry, does not make a person Muslim.

Where it appears: Becoming Muslim — Say it
English: Say it

Where it appears: Becoming Muslim — Say it
English: Say it aloud, in Arabic if you can manage it. If the Arabic is beyond you today, say it in your own language and mean it, then learn the Arabic, because you will say it in every prayer for the rest of your life.

Where it appears: Becoming Muslim — Say it
English: You are Muslim from the moment you say it and mean it. Nobody has to be there, and no imam has to be present.

Where it appears: Becoming Muslim — Say it
English: Getting it written down is a separate question, and worth doing when you can. A mosque or Islamic centre can record it and give you a certificate. Not because your Islam needs one, but because other people's paperwork sometimes does.

Where it appears: Becoming Muslim — Say it
English: These are two different things and the app keeps them apart on purpose. Whether you are Muslim is settled between you and Allah the moment you say it and mean it, and both answers cited here say so plainly, one of them in the words "Islam is a matter that is between a person and his Lord". Whether a registrar, a mosque, a Hajj visa office or a marriage contract will take your word for it later is a paperwork question with a paperwork answer. Historically witnesses were asked for in Muslim courts because inheritance and marriage law followed a person's religion, which is where the idea that they are required comes from. If you are not ready to walk into a mosque, that is fine. None of this expires, and the certificate is available whenever you want it.

Where it appears: Becoming Muslim — You are Muslim
English: You are Muslim

Where it appears: Becoming Muslim — You are Muslim
English: That is it. Nothing else is required of you in this moment, and nothing you did before it is held against you. Becoming Muslim wipes what came before.

Where it appears: Becoming Muslim — You are Muslim
English: You do not need to change your name. You do not need to tell anyone today. Take a full wash when you can, which is recommended for someone who has just become Muslim, and then learn wudu and the prayer, in that order, without rushing.

Where it appears: Clothing — Is this only about women?
English: Is this only about women?

Where it appears: Clothing — Is this only about women?
English: The instruction to lower the gaze and guard modesty is given to men first and then to women, in consecutive verses. That order is worth noticing: modesty in Islam is not a set of rules aimed only at women, and men have their own covering to observe.
Français: L’ordre de baisser le regard et de préserver la pudeur s’adresse d’abord aux hommes, puis aux femmes, dans des versets qui se suivent. Cet ordre mérite d’être remarqué : la pudeur en islam n’est pas un ensemble de règles visant uniquement les femmes, et les hommes ont leur propre part à couvrir.
Español: La orden de bajar la mirada y guardar la modestia se dirige primero a los hombres y luego a las mujeres, en versículos consecutivos. Ese orden merece notarse: la modestia en el islam no es un conjunto de reglas dirigidas solo a las mujeres, y los hombres tienen su propia parte que cubrir.

Where it appears: Clothing — What does it mean for men?
English: What does it mean for men?

Where it appears: Clothing — What does it mean for men?
English: Cover at least from the navel to the knee, keep clothing loose enough not to be revealing, and avoid pure silk and gold jewellery, which the Prophet ﷺ restricted for men. In ordinary Western dress this changes very little in practice.
Français: Couvrez au moins du nombril au genou, portez des vêtements assez amples pour ne rien révéler, et évitez la soie pure et les bijoux en or, que le Prophète ﷺ a interdits aux hommes. Avec des vêtements occidentaux ordinaires, cela change très peu de choses en pratique.
Español: Cubre al menos desde el ombligo hasta la rodilla, lleva ropa lo bastante holgada como para no ser reveladora, y evita la seda pura y las joyas de oro, que el Profeta ﷺ restringió para los hombres. Con la ropa occidental corriente esto cambia muy poco en la práctica.

Where it appears: Clothing — What does it mean for women?
English: What does it mean for women?

Where it appears: Clothing — What does it mean for women?
English: The Qur’an instructs believing women to guard their modesty, to draw their head-coverings over the chest, and to draw their outer garments about them. The commonly taught result is loose clothing covering the body, with the head covered, in front of men outside the immediate family.
Français: Le Coran ordonne aux femmes croyantes de préserver leur pudeur, de rabattre leur voile sur leur poitrine et de se couvrir de leurs grands vêtements. Ce que l’on enseigne habituellement : des vêtements amples couvrant le corps, la tête couverte, devant les hommes extérieurs à la famille proche.
Español: El Corán ordena a las mujeres creyentes guardar su modestia, llevar el velo sobre el pecho y cubrirse con sus mantos. Lo que se enseña habitualmente es ropa holgada que cubra el cuerpo, con la cabeza cubierta, ante hombres ajenos a la familia inmediata.

Where it appears: Clothing — What does it mean for women?
English: Whether the face and hands must also be covered is a long-standing point of scholarly difference, not a settled question.
Français: Savoir si le visage et les mains doivent aussi être couverts est un point de divergence ancien entre les savants, non une question tranchée.
Español: Si el rostro y las manos deben cubrirse también es un punto de diferencia entre los sabios desde hace siglos, no una cuestión zanjada.

Where it appears: Clothing — What does it mean for women?
English: This note used to weigh a majority against a minority, and that count does not hold in either direction. Dorar’s Encyclopedia of Fiqh calls covering the face the view of the majority of scholars, while summaries written from inside the Hanafi and Maliki schools present the opposite as the common position. So the schools are named below rather than counted. You will meet Muslims on both sides who are each following scholarship they trust, and the detail of any one school is worth hearing from someone qualified rather than reading in a summary.

Where it appears: Clothing — What does it mean for women?
English: The face and hands are what ordinarily shows, so covering them is not required in itself, though the school still calls for covering where there is a real fear of harassment.

Where it appears: Clothing — What does it mean for women?
English: The face is not itself among the parts that must be covered, but the position recorded in the school from early on is that it is covered in front of men a woman could marry, because of the harm of not doing so.

Where it appears: Clothing — What does it mean for women?
English: The school carries two positions, and the more predominant of them is that the face is covered in front of men a woman could marry.

Where it appears: Clothing — What does it mean for women?
English: The position the school takes as most correct is that the face and hands are covered in front of men a woman could marry.

Where it appears: Clothing — What does it mean for women?
English: Nobody has the right to pressure you, and starting is often gradual. If covering would put you in danger or out you before you are ready, that is a real circumstance to discuss with someone knowledgeable rather than a rule you are breaking.
Français: Personne n’a le droit de vous faire pression, et cela se fait souvent progressivement. Si vous couvrir vous mettait en danger ou vous exposait avant que vous soyez prête, c’est une situation réelle à discuter avec quelqu’un de compétent, non une règle que vous enfreignez.
Español: Nadie tiene derecho a presionarte, y empezar suele ser gradual. Si cubrirte te pondría en peligro o te expondría antes de que estés preparada, eso es una circunstancia real que hablar con alguien con conocimiento, no una regla que estés incumpliendo.

Where it appears: Clothing — What is the idea behind it?
English: What is the idea behind it?

Where it appears: Clothing — What is the idea behind it?
English: The Qur’an speaks about clothing as something given for covering and for adornment: both, not one at the expense of the other. Islam is not against looking good. The instructions that follow are about modesty in public, not about drabness.

Where it appears: Duʿa and dhikr — What is dhikr?
English: What is dhikr?

Where it appears: Duʿa and dhikr — What is dhikr?
English: Dhikr means remembrance: short phrases repeated through the day. Subḥāna-llāh (glory be to God), al-ḥamdu li-llāh (all praise is God’s), Allāhu akbar (God is greatest). The Qur’an says hearts settle by the remembrance of God, and that is closer to what it does than anything a description manages.

Where it appears: Duʿa and dhikr — What is duʿa?
English: What is duʿa?

Where it appears: Duʿa and dhikr — What is duʿa?
English: Duʿa is simply asking God for something. It has no set form, no required language and no appointed time. The Qur’an says He is near and answers the one who calls. You can make duʿa in English, in your own words, in the car, and it is the same duʿa.

Where it appears: Duʿa and dhikr — What is duʿa?
English: You do not need Arabic for this. The memorised duʿas are worth learning because they are the Prophet’s ﷺ wording, not because your own words would be rejected.
Français: Vous n’avez pas besoin d’arabe pour cela. Les duʿas mémorisées valent la peine d’être apprises parce que ce sont les mots du Prophète ﷺ, non parce que les vôtres seraient rejetés.
Español: No necesitas árabe para esto. Los duʿas memorizados merecen aprenderse porque son las palabras del Profeta ﷺ, no porque las tuyas fueran a ser rechazadas.

Where it appears: Duʿa and dhikr — Where do I start?
English: Where do I start?

Where it appears: Duʿa and dhikr — Where do I start?
English: Pick one phrase and one moment, such as waking or the walk to work. The Everyday duʿas screen has short ones with the Arabic, how it sounds and what it means. The shortest is a single word, which is a deliberate place to begin rather than a compromise.

Where it appears: Duʿa and dhikr — Why does it matter so much?
English: Why does it matter so much?

Where it appears: Duʿa and dhikr — Why does it matter so much?
English: The Prophet ﷺ compared the person who remembers their Lord to the living, and the one who does not to the dead. He also said that whoever says subḥāna-llāhi wa bi-ḥamdih a hundred times in a day has their sins forgiven though they were like the foam of the sea.
Français: Le Prophète ﷺ a comparé celui qui se souvient de son Seigneur aux vivants, et celui qui ne le fait pas aux morts. Il a aussi dit que celui qui dit subḥāna-llāhi wa bi-ḥamdih cent fois par jour voit ses fautes pardonnées, seraient-elles comme l’écume de la mer.
Español: El Profeta ﷺ comparó a quien recuerda a su Señor con los vivos, y a quien no lo hace con los muertos. También dijo que quien dice subḥāna-llāhi wa bi-ḥamdih cien veces al día tiene sus faltas perdonadas aunque fueran como la espuma del mar.

Where it appears: Everyday manners — Are manners really part of it?
English: Are manners really part of it?

Where it appears: Everyday manners — Are manners really part of it?
English: Character sits at the centre rather than the edge. The Prophet ﷺ, described in the Qur’an as being of great character, taught that the best of people are those with the best manners, and the people who lived with him said he never used foul or crude language.

Where it appears: Everyday manners — Is there a summary?
English: Is there a summary?

Where it appears: Everyday manners — Is there a summary?
English: The Prophet ﷺ tied belief directly to behaviour: whoever believes in God and the Last Day should not harm their neighbour, should be generous to their guest, and should say something good or stay quiet. Neighbours, guests, and how you speak. That is a large share of daily life.

Where it appears: Everyday manners — What about talking about people?
English: What about talking about people?

Where it appears: Everyday manners — What about talking about people?
English: The Qur’an forbids mocking others, assuming the worst, spying, and talking about people behind their backs, in two consecutive verses. Backbiting is treated as a serious wrong, not a small one, and it is the habit most people find hardest to drop.

Where it appears: Everyday manners — What do I do when I am angry?
English: What do I do when I am angry?

Where it appears: Everyday manners — What do I do when I am angry?
English: The Prophet ﷺ said the strong person is not the one who overpowers others, but the one who controls himself when angry. It is a redefinition rather than a rule, and it comes up more often than most of the rules do.
Français: Le Prophète ﷺ a dit que le fort n’est pas celui qui terrasse les autres, mais celui qui se maîtrise dans la colère. C’est une redéfinition plus qu’une règle, et elle se présente plus souvent que la plupart des règles.
Español: El Profeta ﷺ dijo que el fuerte no es quien vence a los demás, sino quien se domina a sí mismo cuando está enfadado. Es una redefinición más que una regla, y aparece más a menudo que la mayoría de las reglas.

Where it appears: Everyday manners — What is the measure of it?
English: What is the measure of it?

Where it appears: Everyday manners — What is the measure of it?
English: One of the shortest things the Prophet ﷺ said and one of the hardest: none of you truly believes until he wants for his brother what he wants for himself. It is the test to apply when a situation is not covered by anything you have learned yet.
Français: L’une des paroles les plus brèves du Prophète ﷺ et l’une des plus exigeantes : nul d’entre vous ne croit vraiment tant qu’il n’aime pas pour son frère ce qu’il aime pour lui-même. C’est le test à appliquer quand une situation n’est couverte par rien de ce que vous avez appris.
Español: Una de las cosas más breves que dijo el Profeta ﷺ y de las más difíciles: ninguno de vosotros cree de verdad hasta que quiera para su hermano lo que quiere para sí mismo. Es la prueba que aplicar cuando una situación no está cubierta por nada de lo que has aprendido todavía.

Where it appears: Everyday manners — What is the measure of it?
English: You will get things wrong, in front of people, for a while. Everyone did. Being embarrassed about it is not a sign you are doing badly.
Français: Vous vous tromperez, devant des gens, pendant un temps. Tout le monde est passé par là. En être gêné n’est pas le signe que vous vous en sortez mal.
Español: Te equivocarás, delante de otros, durante un tiempo. A todos les pasó. Que te dé vergüenza no es señal de que lo estés haciendo mal.

English: Prayer

Where it appears: Five Pillars — Prayer
English: Five prayers a day, at set times, facing the Kaʿbah in Mecca.

Where it appears: Five Pillars — Prayer
English: Fajr before sunrise, Dhuhr after midday, ʿAsr in the afternoon, Maghrib just after sunset, and ʿIshaʾ at night. Each one takes a few minutes. You wash first, which is wudu, and the app walks you through both.

Where it appears: Five Pillars — The testimony of faith
English: The testimony of faith

Where it appears: Five Pillars — The testimony of faith
English: Saying, and meaning, that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is His Messenger.

Where it appears: Five Pillars — The testimony of faith
English: This is the pillar the other four rest on. Saying it sincerely is what makes a person Muslim, and it is repeated in every prayer for the rest of your life. It is two statements held together: that worship belongs to Allah alone, and that Muhammad ﷺ is the one who conveyed how.

Where it appears: Food and drink — Is supermarket meat halal?
English: Is supermarket meat halal?

Where it appears: Food and drink — Is supermarket meat halal?
English: People genuinely differ, and you will be told opposite things with equal confidence. The Qur’an permits the food of the People of the Book; what scholars disagree about is whether modern industrial slaughter still resembles what that verse describes. Certified halal meat satisfies every position, which is where most converts start.

Where it appears: Food and drink — Is supermarket meat halal?
English: Muslims in Western countries genuinely differ on supermarket meat, and you will be told opposite things with equal confidence.
Français: Les musulmans des pays occidentaux divergent réellement sur la viande de supermarché, et on vous dira des choses opposées avec la même assurance.
Español: Los musulmanes en países occidentales difieren de verdad sobre la carne del supermercado, y te dirán cosas opuestas con la misma seguridad.

Where it appears: Food and drink — Is supermarket meat halal?
English: The starting point is not in dispute. All four schools hold that meat slaughtered by Jews and Christians is lawful, and all four hold that an animal killed by strangling, electrocution or anything other than cutting the throat was not lawfully slaughtered at all. What people disagree about is whether a modern slaughterhouse still meets that second condition. Stunning, mechanical blades and who is actually doing the slaughtering are all part of it. That makes it a question about how agreed rules apply today rather than a split between the schools, which is why this note names no school and counts nobody: some scholars hold the verse still covers ordinary supermarket meat, and others hold that industrial slaughter no longer resembles what it describes and restrict meat to what is certified. Buying certified halal meat satisfies every position, which is why most converts start there and settle the question later. Nobody is doing anything strange by taking the cautious route while they learn, and nobody is being lax by relying on the verse. The specifics are worth asking someone locally about rather than resolving from an article.

Where it appears: Food and drink — What about eating with my family?
English: What about eating with my family?

Where it appears: Food and drink — What about eating with my family?
English: You do not have to stop eating with people who are not Muslim, and you do not have to make a scene. Eat what you can, quietly leave what you cannot, and answer questions if they come. Most families adjust faster when the change is undramatic.
Français: Vous n’avez pas à cesser de manger avec des personnes non musulmanes, ni à en faire toute une histoire. Mangez ce que vous pouvez, laissez discrètement ce que vous ne pouvez pas, et répondez si on vous questionne. La plupart des familles s’adaptent plus vite quand le changement est discret.
Español: No tienes que dejar de comer con quienes no son musulmanes, ni montar una escena. Come lo que puedas, deja discretamente lo que no, y responde si preguntan. La mayoría de las familias se adapta antes cuando el cambio no es dramático.

Where it appears: Food and drink — What about eating with my family?
English: Utensils that touched pork, or a shared roasting tin, worry converts far more than they worry most scholars. Wash it and move on.
Français: Les ustensiles qui ont touché du porc, ou un plat à four partagé, inquiètent les convertis bien plus que la plupart des savants. Lavez-les et passez à autre chose.
Español: Los cubiertos que tocaron cerdo, o una bandeja de horno compartida, preocupan a los conversos mucho más que a la mayoría de los sabios. Lávalo y sigue adelante.

Where it appears: Food and drink — What changes at the supermarket?
English: What changes at the supermarket?

Where it appears: Food and drink — What changes at the supermarket?
English: Reading labels, for a few weeks. Then it is automatic.

English: What is actually forbidden?

Where it appears: Food and drink — What is actually forbidden?

Where it appears: Ghusl — Intend
English: Intend in your heart that you are washing to lift the state you are in, then say:

Where it appears: Ghusl — Perform wudu
English: Perform wudu

Where it appears: Ghusl — Perform wudu
English: Do a complete wudu as you normally would, including rinsing your mouth and nose. You may leave washing your feet until the very end.

Where it appears: Ghusl — Pour over your head
English: Pour over your head

Where it appears: Ghusl — Pour over your head
English: Pour water over your head three times, working it through your hair until the water reaches the roots and the scalp is wet everywhere.

Where it appears: Ghusl — Pour over your head
English: Long hair does not need undoing for this, but the water has to reach the scalp underneath.

Where it appears: Ghusl — Wash the rest of you
English: Wash the rest of you

Where it appears: Ghusl — Wash the rest of you
English: Pour water over the right side of your body, then the left, until every part of you has been reached: under the arms, behind the ears, between the toes. Nothing may be left dry.

Where it appears: Ghusl — Wash the rest of you
English: Take off anything water cannot pass, such as a ring or a watch, or move it as you go.

Where it appears: Ghusl — Wash your feet
English: If you left your feet until now, wash them, and you are finished.

Where it appears: Ghusl — Wash your feet
English: This ghusl counts as your wudu too. You can pray without repeating it, as long as nothing breaks your wudu afterwards.

Where it appears: Ghusl — Wash your hands
English: Wash both hands up to the wrists, three times.

Where it appears: Ghusl — Wash yourself
English: Wash yourself

Where it appears: Ghusl — Wash yourself
English: Wash the private parts and anywhere else on the body carrying impurity, using your left hand. Then wash your hands again.

Where it appears: Ghusl — When you need it
English: When you need it

Where it appears: Ghusl — When you need it
English: Ghusl is required after sex, whether or not anything was released, and after any release of semen, including in your sleep. It is required when a period ends, and when bleeding after childbirth ends. Until you have done it, wudu is not enough and prayer is not valid.

Where it appears: Ghusl — When you need it
English: It is also recommended, though not required, before Friday prayer, before the two Eids, and for someone who has just become Muslim.

Where it appears: Ghusl — When you need it
English: The thinner, clear fluid that comes with arousal is not the same thing and does not need a ghusl. Wash the part and the clothing it touched, do wudu, and pray.

Where it appears: Ghusl — When you need it
English: `Ali was too shy to ask and sent al-Miqdad to ask for him; the answer was that it requires wudu. This app said "any release of sexual fluid" before, which swept the two together and would have sent people for a full wash they did not owe. The books keep them apart carefully, and so does this.

Where it appears: Ghusl — When you need it
English: Whether the wash on becoming Muslim is required or strongly recommended is a point scholars differ on. Doing it settles the question either way, which is why this app simply says to do it.

Where it appears: Ghusl — When you need it
English: Two reports carry it. Thumamah ibn Uthal, released from the pillar of the mosque, went to a nearby grove, washed, came back and said the shahada. Bukhari files that under a chapter headed "taking a bath on embracing Islam". And Qays ibn `Asim came intending to accept Islam and was told to wash. Scholars read the second differently: some as a command, some as guidance. The recommended reading is the more common one, and it is not only held outside the Hanbali school: a group of Hanbalis report it from Ahmad himself, and al-Mardawi, whose job in that school was to say which position it settles on, chose it. What nobody holds is that your Islam is incomplete without it, and nobody thinks less of you for doing it a week later than the day itself.

Where it appears: Ghusl — When you need it
English: The well-known position of the school holds the full wash obligatory on entering Islam.

Where it appears: Ghusl — When you need it
English: Hold it recommended, unless something else, such as intimacy beforehand, had already made a ghusl due.

Where it appears: Ghusl — When you need it
English: Hold it recommended rather than owed.

Where it appears: Ghusl — When you need it
English: The Friday wash is strongly encouraged rather than owed, and all four schools treat it as a sunnah. The narration that settles it says a wudu on Friday is fine and good, and a ghusl is better.

Where it appears: Ghusl — When you need it
English: This used to be filed here as a difference between "the majority" and "a minority", which was vaguer than the evidence needs. All four schools hold the Friday ghusl a sunnah; the obligatory reading of Bukhari 877, "anyone of you attending the Friday prayer should take a bath", is held outside them. Tirmidhi records ash-Shafi`i's own argument for the first reading: `Umar was addressing the congregation when `Uthman arrived having only done wudu, and `Umar reproached him without sending him back to wash. Neither of them treated it as a condition, and both knew the instruction. One practical point the schools also agree on: it only counts as the Friday wash if it is done before the prayer.

Where it appears: Ghusl — When you need it
English: The Eid wash is a companion's practice more than a narrated command. Ibn `Umar washed on the morning of Eid al-Fitr before setting out, and the practice has been kept ever since.

Where it appears: Ghusl — When you need it
English: The narration that says the Prophet ﷺ himself washed on both Eids is graded weak by Darussalam, so it is not what the recommendation rests on and it is labelled here rather than quietly promoted. What it rests on is Malik's report of Ibn `Umar in the Muwatta. The hadith immediately after the weak one, Ibn Majah 1316, is graded fabricated. The app does not use it and never has.

Where it appears: Halal and haram — Do I need permission for ordinary things?
English: Do I need permission for ordinary things?

Where it appears: Halal and haram — Do I need permission for ordinary things?
English: This is the part people get backwards. Things are permitted unless there is a clear reason otherwise, and the Qur’an describes the Prophet’s ﷺ message as making good things lawful rather than piling on prohibitions. You do not need to find permission for ordinary life.
Français: C’est la partie que l’on comprend à l’envers. Les choses sont permises sauf raison claire du contraire, et le Coran décrit le message du Prophète ﷺ comme rendant licites les bonnes choses plutôt que comme un empilement d’interdits. Vous n’avez pas à chercher une permission pour la vie ordinaire.
Español: Esta es la parte que la gente entiende al revés. Las cosas están permitidas salvo que haya una razón clara en contra, y el Corán describe el mensaje del Profeta ﷺ como algo que hace lícitas las cosas buenas, no que acumula prohibiciones. No necesitas buscar permiso para la vida corriente.

Where it appears: Halal and haram — What about things in between?
English: What about things in between?

Where it appears: Halal and haram — What about things in between?
English: The Prophet ﷺ said the lawful is clear and the unlawful is clear, and between them are matters that are unclear, which many people do not know about. Someone who stays away from what is doubtful protects their faith and their honour. That middle ground is where most real questions live.
Français: Le Prophète ﷺ a dit que le licite est clair et l’illicite est clair, et qu’entre les deux se trouvent des questions ambiguës que beaucoup ignorent. Celui qui s’écarte du douteux préserve sa religion et son honneur. C’est dans cet entre-deux que vivent la plupart des vraies questions.
Español: El Profeta ﷺ dijo que lo lícito está claro y lo ilícito está claro, y entre ambos hay asuntos poco claros que muchos desconocen. Quien se aparta de lo dudoso protege su religión y su honra. En ese terreno intermedio viven casi todas las preguntas reales.

Where it appears: Halal and haram — What about things in between?
English: This is guidance for your own choices, not a licence to police anyone else’s. Being cautious about a doubtful thing for yourself is careful; declaring it forbidden for other people is a different act entirely.
Français: Ceci oriente vos propres choix ; ce n’est pas un permis de surveiller ceux des autres. Être prudent pour soi face à une chose douteuse relève du soin ; la déclarer interdite aux autres est tout autre chose.
Español: Esto orienta tus propias decisiones; no es licencia para vigilar las de nadie más. Ser prudente con algo dudoso por tu cuenta es cuidado; declararlo prohibido para otros es otra cosa muy distinta.

Where it appears: Halal and haram — What do halal and haram mean?
English: What do halal and haram mean?

Where it appears: Halal and haram — What do halal and haram mean?
English: Halal means permitted. Haram means forbidden. They apply to everything, not just food: how you earn money, how you speak about people, what you wear. Most of life is halal and always was; the forbidden list is short.

Where it appears: Halal and haram — What if I am not sure?
English: What if I am not sure?

Where it appears: Halal and haram — What if I am not sure?
English: Ask someone qualified, and ask about your actual situation rather than the general case, because circumstances change answers. You will also meet Muslims who are certain of opposite answers on the same question. That usually means it is a genuine point of scholarly difference rather than that one of them is lying to you.

Where it appears: Isha — Face the qibla and intend
English: Stand facing the qibla, feet roughly shoulder-width apart, and intend in your heart that you are praying Isha.

Where it appears: Isha — Turn to your left
English: That is Isha complete.

Where it appears: Istikhara — Face the qibla and intend
English: Stand facing the qibla, feet roughly shoulder-width apart, and intend in your heart that you are praying Istikhara.

Where it appears: Istikhara — Then ask
English: Then ask

Where it appears: Istikhara — Then ask
English: The prayer is finished. Still sitting, say the duʿa, and where it says “this matter”, name the thing you are deciding.

Where it appears: Istikhara — Then ask
English: That is Istikhara complete.

Where it appears: Losing count in prayer — I have lost count. What now?
English: I have lost count. What now?

Where it appears: Losing count in prayer — I have lost count. What now?
English: If you cannot remember whether you are on the second or third rakʿah, assume the smaller one, the number you are certain of, and carry on from there.

Where it appears: Losing count in prayer — I have lost count. What now?
English: Do not start the prayer again. Restarting is the common instinct and it is not the answer.

Where it appears: Losing count in prayer — It keeps happening. Is that bad?
English: It keeps happening. Is that bad?

Where it appears: Losing count in prayer — It keeps happening. Is that bad?
English: Everyone loses count, including people who have prayed all their lives. If the doubt keeps coming back in the same prayer, ignore it and finish. Chasing certainty is itself a distraction from the prayer.

Where it appears: Losing count in prayer — What are the two extra prostrations?
English: What are the two extra prostrations?

Where it appears: Losing count in prayer — What are the two extra prostrations?
English: Finish the prayer as normal. Before or after the final taslim, make two prostrations just as you do in the prayer itself, saying the takbir as you go down and as you come up, then give the taslim.

Where it appears: Losing count in prayer — What are the two extra prostrations?
English: Schools differ on whether these come before or after the taslim. Either is taught by scholars; do it the way whoever taught you does it.

Where it appears: Losing count in prayer — What else does that fix cover?
English: What else does that fix cover?

Where it appears: Losing count in prayer — What else does that fix cover?
English: Those two prostrations also cover forgetting the first sitting, adding a movement by mistake, or saying something in the wrong place.

Where it appears: Maghrib — Face the qibla and intend
English: Stand facing the qibla, feet roughly shoulder-width apart, and intend in your heart that you are praying Maghrib.

Where it appears: Maghrib — Turn to your left
English: That is Maghrib complete.

Where it appears: Missing a prayer — I missed a prayer. Is that a sin?
English: I missed a prayer. Is that a sin?

Where it appears: Missing a prayer — I missed a prayer. Is that a sin?
English: Sleeping through a prayer or forgetting it is not a sin. You pray it as soon as you wake or remember, and that prayer counts as the one you missed.

Where it appears: Missing a prayer — What if I missed several?
English: What if I missed several?

Where it appears: Missing a prayer — What if I missed several?
English: Missed more than one? Pray them in the order they were due, then the prayer you are currently in time for.

Where it appears: Missing a prayer — What if it keeps happening?
English: What if it keeps happening?

Where it appears: Missing a prayer — What if it keeps happening?
English: The thing that ends people’s prayer is not the prayer they missed. It is deciding they are now the sort of person who misses prayers. Pray the next one. That is the whole recovery.

Where it appears: Missing a prayer — What if it keeps happening?
English: Deliberately leaving a prayer is a serious matter and different from oversleeping. The action is still the same: pray it, and pray the next one.

Where it appears: Patience and gratitude — Does patience mean doing nothing?
English: Does patience mean doing nothing?

Where it appears: Patience and gratitude — Does patience mean doing nothing?
English: Sabr means holding steady: carrying on doing the right thing while something is hard, rather than accepting whatever happens. The Qur’an pairs it with prayer as the two things to seek help through, which is a practical instruction more than a moral one: when it is bad, pray.

Where it appears: Patience and gratitude — What does gratitude actually mean?
English: What does gratitude actually mean?

Where it appears: Patience and gratitude — What does gratitude actually mean?
English: The Qur’an says that if you are grateful, He will increase you. Much of gratitude in practice is simply naming things, which is why al-ḥamdu li-llāh is said constantly, over small things, out loud. It is a habit of attention rather than a feeling you wait for.

Where it appears: Patience and gratitude — What does this look like for me now?
English: What does this look like for me now?

Where it appears: Patience and gratitude — What does this look like for me now?
English: The first year often costs something real: family who do not understand, friends who drift, a life that has to be rearranged. That difficulty is not a sign you chose wrongly, and it is exactly the situation the word sabr is for.

Where it appears: Patience and gratitude — Why are these always paired?
English: Why are these always paired?

Where it appears: Patience and gratitude — Why are these always paired?
English: The Prophet ﷺ said the believer’s situation is remarkable, because everything that happens to them is good: when something pleasant comes they are grateful and that is good for them, and when something painful comes they are patient and that is good for them. Nobody else, he said, is in that position.
Français: Le Prophète ﷺ a dit que la situation du croyant est remarquable, car tout ce qui lui arrive est un bien : quand vient une chose agréable il remercie, et c’est un bien pour lui ; quand vient une chose douloureuse il patiente, et c’est un bien pour lui. Personne d’autre, a-t-il dit, n’est dans cette situation.
Español: El Profeta ﷺ dijo que la situación del creyente es admirable, porque todo lo que le ocurre es bueno: cuando llega algo agradable da gracias y eso es bueno para él, y cuando llega algo doloroso tiene paciencia y eso es bueno para él. Nadie más, dijo, está en esa posición.

Where it appears: Periods and prayer — Do I still pray?
English: Do I still pray?

Where it appears: Periods and prayer — Do I still pray?
English: From the moment bleeding starts until it stops, you do not pray. This is not permission to skip. You are not supposed to pray, and praying anyway is not better.

Where it appears: Periods and prayer — Do I still pray?
English: You do not make these prayers up afterwards. They are not a debt. This surprises most people, so it is worth saying twice: they are simply not owed.

Where it appears: Periods and prayer — What about after giving birth?
English: What about after giving birth?

Where it appears: Periods and prayer — What about after giving birth?
English: Bleeding after childbirth follows the same rules as a period: you do not pray, you do not make those prayers up, and you take a ghusl when it ends.

Where it appears: Periods and prayer — What about fasting?
English: What about fasting?

Where it appears: Periods and prayer — What about fasting?
English: You do not fast during a period. Fasts missed in Ramadan for this reason are made up later, before the next Ramadan, at your own pace.

Where it appears: Periods and prayer — What about fasting?
English: Prayer and fasting work differently here. Prayers are not made up; fasts are.

Where it appears: Periods and prayer — What can I still do?
English: What can I still do?

Where it appears: Periods and prayer — What can I still do?
English: Everything else stays open to you. You can make duʿa in your own words, say dhikr, listen to the Qur’an, go on learning, and sit with people who are praying.

Where it appears: Periods and prayer — What can I still do?
English: You are not unclean and you are not excluded. The rest from prayer is a concession you have been given, not a punishment or a mark against you.

Where it appears: Periods and prayer — What if the bleeding is not a period?
English: What if the bleeding is not a period?

Where it appears: Periods and prayer — What if the bleeding is not a period?
English: Bleeding outside your normal pattern, or lasting far beyond it, is treated differently, and it does not stop you praying. A woman asked the Prophet ﷺ exactly this and was told not to give up her prayers, because that bleeding comes from a blood vessel rather than being a period. You wash, do wudu, and pray; the wudu is done afresh for each prayer.

Where it appears: Periods and prayer — What if the bleeding is not a period?
English: Telling the two apart is genuinely a question for someone knowledgeable, not for an app. Do not guess, and do not stop praying on a guess.

Where it appears: Periods and prayer — When do I start praying again?
English: When do I start praying again?

Where it appears: Periods and prayer — When do I start praying again?
English: Once the bleeding has stopped, take a ghusl, the full wash, and you go straight back to praying with the next prayer due.

Where it appears: Periods and prayer — Why do people tell me different things?
English: Why do people tell me different things?

Where it appears: Periods and prayer — Why do people tell me different things?
English: One question here is genuinely open and two are not, and it saves a lot of confusion to know which is which. Reciting the Qur’an during a period is the open one: scholars divide on it, and you will meet people certain of opposite answers. Holding a printed muṣḥaf is not open in the same way, because all four schools say not to. Nor is sitting in the prayer hall of a mosque, which all four treat as somewhere not to stay through a period, though several allow walking through.

Where it appears: Periods and prayer — Why do people tell me different things?
English: None of this touches what the last section said. Listening, duʿa, dhikr and learning are open on every account, and nobody who tells you one of these is being difficult with you.

Where it appears: Periods and prayer — Why do people tell me different things?
English: On reciting the Qur’an there is no settled answer, and both sides are held by people who know exactly what they are doing.

Where it appears: Periods and prayer — Why do people tell me different things?
English: This section used to say scholars differ on all three of these and give no positions, which put a question all four schools agree on next to one they genuinely split over. On the muṣḥaf the agreement is about touching it; scholars treat a barrier between hand and page differently, so if you need to carry one or turn its pages, that is the thing to ask about. On the mosque the agreement is about remaining there. The Shafi`i and Hanbali schools permit passing through, and several contemporary scholars go further. If any of it affects your week, ask someone knowledgeable which position your local mosque follows.

Where it appears: Periods and prayer — Why do people tell me different things?
English: Permit reciting during a period, which is also al-Shafi`i’s earlier position and one narration from Ahmad.

Where it appears: Periods and prayer — Why do people tell me different things?
English: The settled positions of the Hanafi, Shafi`i and Hanbali schools hold back from reciting until the period ends.

Where it appears: Periods and prayer — Why do people tell me different things?
English: Ibn Taymiyyah, Ibn al-Qayyim and Ibn `Uthaymin took the permitting view, and it is the verdict of the Permanent Committee.

Where it appears: Phrase: Akhī · Ukhtī
English: My brother · my sister.

Where it appears: Praying at night — How do I actually start?
English: How do I actually start?

Where it appears: Praying at night — How do I actually start?
English: Set an alarm twenty minutes before Fajr rather than for the middle of the night. You are already going to be awake for Fajr; this is standing up a little earlier. Starting there is why people keep it.

Where it appears: Praying at night — How little counts?
English: How little counts?

Where it appears: Praying at night — How little counts?
English: There is no minimum to reach and no number to work up to. Two rakʿahs, on one night, is the thing itself. People who pray it for decades mostly pray a little, often, which is the pattern the Prophet ﷺ described as the deeds God loves most, the small ones kept up.

Where it appears: Praying at night — How little counts?
English: It is the same prayer you already know. Nothing about the movements or the words changes. Only the time, and that you chose to be there.

Where it appears: Praying at night — What if I have not slept?
English: What if I have not slept?

Where it appears: Praying at night — What if I have not slept?
English: Tahajjud is prayed after waking, which is what separates it from simply staying up late. If you have not slept, you are praying qiyam al-layl, which is also good, also voluntary, and not what this word means.

Where it appears: Praying at night — What is tahajjud?
English: What is tahajjud?

Where it appears: Praying at night — What is tahajjud?
English: A prayer in the last part of the night, after you have slept and before Fajr. The Qur’an tells the Prophet ﷺ to keep part of the night for it as something additional, and that word matters: it is not owed. Nobody is behind for not praying it.

Where it appears: Praying when you cannot stand — Does it count the same?
English: Does it count the same?

Where it appears: Praying when you cannot stand — Does it count the same?
English: A prayer prayed sitting because you could not stand is not worth less than one prayed standing. It is the prayer you were asked for.

Where it appears: Praying when you cannot stand — How do I bow and prostrate?
English: How do I bow and prostrate?

Where it appears: Praying when you cannot stand — How do I bow and prostrate?
English: Lean forward a little for the bowing, and further forward for the prostration, so that the prostration is clearly lower than the bow. Say everything exactly as you would standing.

Where it appears: Praying when you cannot stand — What if I cannot sit either?
English: What if I cannot sit either?

Where it appears: Praying when you cannot stand — What if I cannot sit either?
English: Pray lying on your right side facing the qibla, or on your back, and make the movements with your head or your eyes. Prayer is never dropped for illness while you are conscious.

Where it appears: Praying when you cannot stand — What if I cannot stand?
English: What if I cannot stand?

Where it appears: Praying when you cannot stand — What if I cannot stand?
English: If standing is beyond you, or would cause real pain or harm, pray sitting down, on a chair or on the floor, whichever you can manage.

Where it appears: Praying while travelling — Can I pray two together?
English: Can I pray two together?

Where it appears: Praying while travelling — Can I pray two together?
English: You may also pray Dhuhr and ʿAsr together, and Maghrib and ʿIshaʾ together, at the time of either one of the pair.

Where it appears: Praying while travelling — How far counts as travelling?
English: How far counts as travelling?

Where it appears: Praying while travelling — How far counts as travelling?
English: Far enough that you would ordinarily call it travelling. There is no distance in the Qur’an or in any narration, so scholars have had to draw the line themselves, and they draw it in different places. The most common answer works out at somewhere around eighty to ninety kilometres. What everyone agrees on is when it starts: not when you decide to go, but once you have actually left the place you live.

Where it appears: Praying while travelling — How far counts as travelling?
English: A daily commute is not a journey, however long it feels. If you are unsure, ask someone locally rather than deciding alone.

Where it appears: Praying while travelling — How far counts as travelling?
English: No verse and no narration gives a distance. The figure most scholars use is a conversion of a classical measure, and a second position holds there is no fixed distance at all: if it is a journey, you may shorten.

Where it appears: Praying while travelling — How far counts as travelling?
English: The app used to say "roughly eighty kilometres" without saying where the number came from, which made a scholarly conversion look like a reported figure. A barid is a classical measure of distance, and four of them is two days of loaded-camel travel; converted into modern units it lands near eighty-eight kilometres, and different conversions give slightly different numbers, which is most of why you will hear eighty from one person and ninety from another. How long you may keep shortening once you arrive is a second difference again. The Maliki and Shafi`i schools stop at four days, the Hanafi school at fifteen, and some hold there is no limit while you have not settled.

Where it appears: Praying while travelling — How far counts as travelling?
English: The Maliki, Shafi`i and Hanbali schools put it at four burud, which converts to roughly eighty-eight kilometres.

Where it appears: Praying while travelling — How far counts as travelling?
English: Reckon it from a journey of about three days at the pace people travelled then, which the school gives as forty-eight miles, or roughly seventy-seven kilometres.

Where it appears: Praying while travelling — How far counts as travelling?
English: Ibn Taymiyyah, Ibn al-Qayyim and Ibn `Uthaymin held there is no fixed distance: anything ordinarily called travelling counts.

Where it appears: Praying while travelling — How much do I pray when travelling?
English: How much do I pray when travelling?

Where it appears: Praying while travelling — How much do I pray when travelling?
English: On a journey, the four-rakʿah prayers, Dhuhr, ʿAsr and ʿIshaʾ, are prayed as two. Fajr stays two and Maghrib stays three.

Where it appears: Praying while travelling — How much do I pray when travelling?
English: This is a gift, not a compromise. It is the practice of the Prophet ﷺ on journeys, not a lowering of the bar.

Where it appears: Ramadan — What are suhoor and iftar?
English: What are suhoor and iftar?

Where it appears: Ramadan — What are suhoor and iftar?
English: Suhoor is the meal before dawn. The Prophet ﷺ said to take it, because there is blessing in it, and skipping it makes a long day much harder. Iftar is breaking the fast at sunset, traditionally with dates and water, and he taught not to delay it once the sun is down.

Where it appears: Ramadan — What does the fast involve?
English: What does the fast involve?

Where it appears: Ramadan — What does the fast involve?
English: From first light until sunset, no food, no drink, not even water, and no sexual intimacy. The Qur’an marks the start of the fast as the moment dawn becomes distinguishable, and the end at sunset. Outside those hours you eat and drink normally.

Where it appears: Ramadan — What happens at the end?
English: What happens at the end?

Where it appears: Ramadan — What happens at the end?
English: The month ends with Eid: a morning prayer, new or good clothes, and visiting people. Before that prayer, every Muslim gives a small fixed amount of food so that nobody is left out of the day. It is called zakat al-fitr and it is due for every member of a household, old and young, and paid on behalf of anyone in your care.

Where it appears: Ramadan — What happens at the end?
English: Whether it may be given as money instead of food is a real difference, and it decides what you actually hand over. Most mosques and charities collect it either way and will tell you which they are doing.

Where it appears: Ramadan — What happens at the end?
English: Nothing about your Eid depends on getting this right in your first year. Give it through whoever your local mosque collects for, in the form they ask for, before the Eid prayer. That satisfies the position they follow, and the timing is the part the narration is strictest about.

Where it appears: Ramadan — What happens at the end?
English: Allow the value in money, and consider it easier for the recipient.

Where it appears: Ramadan — What happens at the end?
English: Malik, ash-Shafi`i and Ahmad hold that it is the staple food the narration names, given as food rather than as its value.

Where it appears: Ramadan — What happens the rest of the month?
English: What happens the rest of the month?

Where it appears: Ramadan — What happens the rest of the month?
English: Mosques fill up for taraweeh, a long optional night prayer, and many people read far more Qur’an than usual. Jibril would go through the Qur’an with the Prophet ﷺ each night of Ramadan. There is also more giving: he was described as at his most generous this month.

Where it appears: Ramadan — What is Laylat al-Qadr?
English: What is Laylat al-Qadr?

Where it appears: Ramadan — What is Laylat al-Qadr?
English: One night in Ramadan is called Laylat al-Qadr, the Night of Decree, the night the Qur’an began to be revealed, which the Qur’an says is better than a thousand months. Nobody is told which night it is. The Prophet ﷺ said to look for it in the odd nights of the last ten, which is why mosques fill up at the end of the month.

Where it appears: Ramadan — What is Ramadan?
English: What is Ramadan?

Where it appears: Ramadan — What is Ramadan?
English: The ninth month of the Islamic lunar calendar, and the month in which the Qur’an began to be revealed. Because the calendar is lunar, it moves about eleven days earlier each year, so it passes through every season over a lifetime.

Where it appears: Ramadan — Who does not have to fast?
English: Who does not have to fast?

Where it appears: Ramadan — Who does not have to fast?
English: The Qur’an names two: anyone ill, and anyone travelling. Both make the days up afterwards, at their own pace, before the next Ramadan. It also gives a second route for someone who could only fast with real hardship: feeding a poor person for each day instead of fasting it. That second route is the answer for a long-term or permanent condition, where making the days up later is not something that is ever going to happen. During a period a woman does not fast either, and those days are made up.

Where it appears: Ramadan — Who does not have to fast?
English: If you are on medication or managing an illness, ask a doctor and someone knowledgeable before your first Ramadan rather than during it. A first Ramadan is far more often damaged by someone fasting who should not have than by someone taking an exemption they were given.

Where it appears: Ramadan — Who does not have to fast?
English: Not fasting when you are exempt is not a failure and not something to feel guilty about. The exemption is part of the instruction, not a loophole in it.
Français: Ne pas jeûner quand vous en êtes dispensé n’est pas un échec et n’a pas à vous culpabiliser. La dispense fait partie de la consigne, ce n’est pas une faille dedans.
Español: No ayunar cuando estás exento no es un fracaso ni algo por lo que sentirse culpable. La exención forma parte de la indicación, no es un resquicio en ella.

Where it appears: Ramadan — Who does not have to fast?
English: Pregnancy and breastfeeding are the case scholars genuinely divide over. That you may stop fasting where there is real risk to you or the baby is agreed; what you owe afterwards is not, and the answer can turn on whether the worry was for you or for the child.

Where it appears: Ramadan — Who does not have to fast?
English: This lesson used to say the exemptions were covered by "makes the days up later", which is one of these four answers stated as though it were the ruling. There is a fifth position that is older than all of them: Ibn `Abbas and Ibn `Umar held that a pregnant or breastfeeding woman feeds a poor person for each day and does not make the days up at all, which is the gentlest of the answers and is still taught. Among contemporary scholars, Ibn Baz, Ibn `Uthaymin and the Permanent Committee held that the days are made up. Nothing here needs deciding in the abstract: work out with someone knowledgeable what applies to your own situation, and do it before Ramadan rather than in the middle of it.

Where it appears: Ramadan — Who does not have to fast?
English: Make the days up, and nothing else is owed.

Where it appears: Ramadan — Who does not have to fast?
English: A pregnant woman makes the days up. A breastfeeding woman makes them up and also feeds a poor person for each day.

Where it appears: Ramadan — Who does not have to fast?
English: If she stopped fasting out of fear for herself, she makes the days up. If out of fear for the child alone, she makes them up and feeds a poor person for each day.

Where it appears: Ramadan — Who does not have to fast?
English: The same distinction as the Shafi`i school.

Where it appears: Ramadan — Who does not have to fast?
English: Feeding a poor person for each missed day is what "fidyah" means when you hear the word. Most mosques and Muslim charities collect it and will tell you the amount they use locally.

Where it appears: Ramadan — Why fast at all?
English: Why fast at all?

Where it appears: Ramadan — Why fast at all?
English: The Qur’an gives the reason directly: so that you may become mindful of God. It is not endurance for its own sake, and it is not a diet. Being hungry at four in the afternoon is a reminder of who provides, and of people for whom that hunger is not a choice.
Français: Le Coran en donne directement la raison : afin que vous deveniez conscients de Dieu. Ce n’est pas de l’endurance pour elle-même, et ce n’est pas un régime. Avoir faim à quatre heures de l’après-midi rappelle qui pourvoit, et rappelle ceux pour qui cette faim n’est pas un choix.
Español: El Corán da la razón directamente: para que seáis conscientes de Dios. No es resistencia por sí misma, y no es una dieta. Tener hambre a las cuatro de la tarde recuerda quién provee, y a quienes esa hambre no la eligen.
