Where it appears: Six Articles — Belief in Allah
English: Belief in Allah

Where it appears: Six Articles — Belief in Allah
English: That Allah is one, without partner, and that nothing else deserves worship.

Where it appears: Six Articles — Belief in Allah
English: The other five sit inside this one. It is not only accepting that God exists. It is accepting that He is one, that nothing shares His authority, and that worship is owed to Him alone. Everything you say in prayer is a restatement of it.

Where it appears: Six Articles — Belief in divine decree
English: Belief in divine decree

Where it appears: Six Articles — Belief in divine decree
English: That nothing happens outside Allah’s knowledge and will, the good and the hard alike.

Where it appears: Six Articles — Belief in divine decree
English: This is the one people find hardest, and it is usually misread as meaning your choices do not matter. It does not. You still choose, and you are still answerable for what you choose. Held rightly it settles you rather than paralyses you: you act as well as you can, and you are not crushed by the part of the outcome that was never yours to control.

Where it appears: Six Articles — Belief in divine decree
English: If this one sits badly with you at first, that is normal and it is not a sign your faith is faulty. It is the article scholars have written the most about, precisely because it is difficult.

Where it appears: Six Articles — Belief in the angels
English: Belief in the angels

Where it appears: Six Articles — Belief in the angels
English: That Allah created angels, who carry out what He commands.

Where it appears: Six Articles — Belief in the angels
English: Angels are created beings. They are not divine, not partners of Allah, and not prayed to. Jibril, who brought the revelation to the Prophet ﷺ, is the one you will hear named most often. You are not asked to picture them or explain them, only to accept that they are real.

Where it appears: Six Articles — Belief in the Last Day
English: Belief in the Last Day

Where it appears: Six Articles — Belief in the Last Day
English: That this life ends, everyone is raised, and each person answers for what they did.

Where it appears: Six Articles — Belief in the Last Day
English: Nothing you do is lost or goes unweighed, including what nobody else ever saw. When the Day comes is known only to Allah. Working out dates for it is not part of believing in it, and people who claim to have done so are to be ignored.

Where it appears: Six Articles — Belief in the messengers
English: Belief in the messengers

Where it appears: Six Articles — Belief in the messengers
English: That Allah sent prophets to every people, and that Muhammad ﷺ is the last of them.

Where it appears: Six Articles — Belief in the messengers
English: Many of them will already be familiar: Ibrahim, Musa, ʿIsa, and others shared with Judaism and Christianity. Islam honours them as men Allah sent, not as divine, and does not let you accept some and reject others. Muhammad ﷺ closes the line; no prophet comes after him.

Where it appears: Six Articles — Belief in the revealed books
English: Belief in the revealed books

Where it appears: Six Articles — Belief in the revealed books
English: That Allah sent scripture to guide people, and that the Qur’an is the last of it.

Where it appears: Six Articles — Belief in the revealed books
English: The Qur’an names earlier revelations, among them the Tawrat given to Musa and the Injil given to ʿIsa. Believing in them means believing Allah sent them. It does not mean the texts other faiths read today are those revelations as they were sent.

Where it appears: Standing at night — How do I finish?
English: How do I finish?

Where it appears: Standing at night — How do I finish?
English: Whatever you pray at night, end it with witr, a single rakʿah that makes the night’s total odd. It is what closes the night prayer.

Where it appears: Standing at night — How is it different from tahajjud?
English: How is it different from tahajjud?

Where it appears: Standing at night — How is it different from tahajjud?
English: Whether you slept. Pray at night before sleeping and it is qiyam al-layl; sleep first, wake, and pray, and that is tahajjud. Both are voluntary, both are the same movements, and nobody is doing the lesser one.

Where it appears: Standing at night — How is it different from tahajjud?
English: This is the whole difference. If you are unsure which you prayed, it does not affect whether it counted.

Where it appears: Standing at night — What is qiyam al-layl?
English: What is qiyam al-layl?

Where it appears: Standing at night — What is qiyam al-layl?
English: Praying at night, before you have slept. Any amount, any part of the night after Isha. It is the same prayer you already know: two rakʿahs at a time, as many times as you want.

Where it appears: Standing at night — Where will I hear the word?
English: Where will I hear the word?

Where it appears: Standing at night — Where will I hear the word?
English: In Ramadan, mosques announce “qiyam” for the long night prayers in the last ten nights. Taraweeh is the same family of prayer. You are welcome at it, you can leave when you need to, and nobody is counting your rakʿahs.

Where it appears: Tahajjud — Face the qibla and intend
English: Stand facing the qibla, feet roughly shoulder-width apart, and intend in your heart that you are praying Tahajjud.

Where it appears: Tahajjud — Turn to your left
English: That is Tahajjud complete.

Where it appears: Tayammum — Intend
English: Intend in your heart that you are purifying yourself for prayer, in place of using water.

Where it appears: Tayammum — Touch the ground
English: Touch the ground

Where it appears: Tayammum — Touch the ground
English: Place both palms flat on a clean natural surface: earth, sand, stone, or dust settled on something. Lift them and shake off any excess.

Where it appears: Tayammum — Touch the ground
English: It does not have to be soil. A dusty windowsill or a stone wall will do.

Where it appears: Tayammum — When it ends
English: When it ends

Where it appears: Tayammum — When it ends
English: Tayammum breaks for the same reasons wudu breaks, and it ends the moment water becomes available to you.

Where it appears: Tayammum — When you can use it
English: When you can use it

Where it appears: Tayammum — When you can use it
English: Tayammum replaces wudu, and replaces ghusl, when there is no water you can reach, when using it would make you ill or make an illness worse, or when the only water available is needed for drinking.

Where it appears: Tayammum — When you can use it
English: It is not for when water is merely inconvenient. But it is genuinely allowed when it applies, and people miss prayers they were permitted to pray.

Where it appears: Tayammum — Wipe your face
English: Wipe your face

Where it appears: Tayammum — Wipe your face
English: Wipe both palms once over your whole face.

Where it appears: Tayammum — Wipe your hands
English: Wipe your hands

Where it appears: Tayammum — Wipe your hands
English: Wipe the back of your right hand to the wrist with your left palm, then the back of your left hand with your right. You are finished and may pray.

Where it appears: Tayammum — Wipe your hands
English: Some schools wipe the arms to the elbows instead of stopping at the wrists. Both are taught by scholars; you will see people do it either way.

Where it appears: Tayammum — Wipe your hands
English: In the narration the Prophet ﷺ struck the earth once, blew the dust off, and wiped the face and the backs of the hands. The two wordings Bukhari carries put those in either order, which is why you will see both taught. This guide follows the order of the wudu verse: face, then hands. Schools that teach wiping to the elbows argue from other narrations and from that same verse. Nobody will think you have prayed invalidly either way.

Where it appears: The Muslim year — How does this affect my week?
English: How does this affect my week?

Where it appears: The Muslim year — How does this affect my week?
English: For most of the year, not at all — you will pick the date up from the people around you and never need to work it out. It only matters at the two ends of Ramadan, and there it is announced locally rather than calculated in advance, so mosques in the same city can start the month or the Eid a day apart. That is normal and not worth worrying about.

Where it appears: The Muslim year — How does this affect my week?
English: Whether a month begins by sighting the moon locally or by astronomical calculation is a live question, and communities in the same country sometimes start Ramadan on different days.
Français: Savoir si un mois commence par l’observation locale de la lune ou par le calcul astronomique est une question vive, et des communautés d’un même pays commencent parfois le Ramadan à des jours différents.
Español: Si un mes empieza por la observación local de la luna o por cálculo astronómico es una cuestión viva, y comunidades del mismo país empiezan Ramadán a veces en días distintos.

Where it appears: The Muslim year — How does this affect my week?
English: Both approaches are argued from evidence and neither community is being careless. As a beginner the practical answer is to follow the mosque or community you pray with. Scholars have discussed this in more detail.
Français: Les deux approches s’argumentent par des preuves et aucune communauté n’est négligente. Pour un débutant, la réponse pratique est de suivre la mosquée ou la communauté avec laquelle il prie. Les savants ont traité cela plus en détail.
Español: Ambos enfoques se argumentan con pruebas y ninguna comunidad está siendo descuidada. Para un principiante la respuesta práctica es seguir a la mezquita o comunidad con la que reza. Los sabios han tratado esto con más detalle.

Where it appears: The Muslim year — How does this affect my week?
English: Follow the sighting of the moon, as reported locally or regionally.
Français: Suivre l’observation de la lune, telle qu’elle est rapportée localement ou dans la région.
Español: Seguir la observación de la luna, según se informe localmente o en la región.

Where it appears: The Muslim year — How does this affect my week?
English: Some bodies accept astronomical calculation to fix the date in advance.
Français: Certaines instances acceptent le calcul astronomique pour fixer la date à l’avance.
Español: Algunos organismos aceptan el cálculo astronómico para fijar la fecha por adelantado.

Where it appears: The Muslim year — What are the sacred months?
English: What are the sacred months?

Where it appears: The Muslim year — What are the sacred months?
English: The Qur’an says four of the twelve are sacred, and the Prophet ﷺ named them in his farewell sermon: three consecutive ones, Dhul-Qaʿdah, Dhul-Hijjah and Muharram, and Rajab. Fighting is prohibited in them, and wrongdoing in them is treated as more serious.

Where it appears: The Muslim year — What are the twelve months?
English: What are the twelve months?

Where it appears: The Muslim year — What are the twelve months?
English: In order, from the top of the year. Four are sacred, two carry an Eid and one carries the fast; the other five have nothing in them at all. Several are named for a season they no longer fall in — Rabiʿ is spring, Jumada is the dry part of the year — because the months kept moving and the names did not.

Where it appears: The Muslim year — What are the twelve months?
English: You may hear that Safar is an unlucky month, or that it is a bad time to marry or travel. That is a pre-Islamic superstition, and the Prophet ﷺ named it and rejected it. No month carries bad luck.

Where it appears: The Muslim year — Which months ask anything of me?
English: Which months ask anything of me?

Where it appears: The Muslim year — Which months ask anything of me?
English: Only one thing in the year is obligatory, and it is Ramadan, which has a lesson of its own. Four others are worth knowing because you will hear all four mentioned and none of them is required: the fast of ʿAshuraʾ on the tenth of Muharram, which the Prophet ﷺ kept and which became voluntary once Ramadan was prescribed; fasting through Shaʿban, which he did more of than in any month but Ramadan; six fasts spread through Shawwal after Ramadan; and the first ten days of Dhul-Hijjah, which he described as the best days of the year for doing good.

Where it appears: The Muslim year — Why does the date move every year?
English: Why does the date move every year?

Where it appears: The Muslim year — Why does the date move every year?
English: Twelve months, each beginning with a new moon, making a year about eleven days shorter than the solar one. That is why Ramadan and the two Eids move earlier every year rather than falling on fixed dates. Over a lifetime they pass through every season.

Where it appears: The prayer after a sin — Do I have to pray it to be forgiven?
English: Do I have to pray it to be forgiven?

Where it appears: The prayer after a sin — Do I have to pray it to be forgiven?
English: You are forgiven by turning back to God and meaning it. There is no ceremony and nothing to perform. This prayer is something you may do, not a step you have missed. It exists because doing something with your body often helps when saying it in your head does not.

Where it appears: The prayer after a sin — Do I have to pray it to be forgiven?
English: There is no limit, and no shame in praying it often. Somebody who prays it twice in a week has not failed twice. They have turned back twice.

Where it appears: The prayer after a sin — What is it for?
English: What is it for?

Where it appears: The prayer after a sin — What is it for?
English: Abu Bakr reported that the Prophet ﷺ said no one does something wrong, then gets up and purifies himself, then prays, then asks God’s forgiveness, except that God forgives him. Wudu, two rakʿahs, and asking. That is the whole of it.

Where it appears: The prayer of repentance — Face the qibla and intend
English: Stand facing the qibla, feet roughly shoulder-width apart, and intend in your heart that you are praying The prayer of repentance.

Where it appears: The prayer of repentance — Turn to your left
English: That is The prayer of repentance complete.

Where it appears: What breaks the prayer — Can I move at all?
English: Can I move at all?

Where it appears: What breaks the prayer — Can I move at all?
English: Scratching, shifting your weight, stepping forward to close a gap, picking up a child: none of this ends the prayer. What is meant by movement breaking it is a lot of it, continuously, for no reason connected to praying. The Prophet ﷺ prayed while carrying his granddaughter, putting her down to prostrate and picking her back up.

Where it appears: What breaks the prayer — What about ordinary mistakes?
English: What about ordinary mistakes?

Where it appears: What breaks the prayer — What about ordinary mistakes?
English: Losing count, forgetting a sitting, adding a movement, saying something in the wrong place: none of these break the prayer. They are fixed with two extra prostrations at the end, which the app covers separately. A beginner will do all of these, and none of them is a disaster.

Where it appears: What breaks the prayer — What about ordinary mistakes?
English: The most common beginner mistake is starting the prayer over. Almost nothing requires that, and restarting turns a small slip into a long one.
Français: L’erreur la plus courante du débutant est de recommencer la prière. Presque rien ne l’exige, et recommencer transforme un petit écart en un long.
Español: El error más común del principiante es volver a empezar la oración. Casi nada lo exige, y reiniciar convierte un desliz pequeño en uno largo.

Where it appears: What breaks the prayer — What actually breaks it?
English: What actually breaks it?

Where it appears: What breaks the prayer — What actually breaks it?
English: Losing your wudu. Speaking on purpose to someone. Eating or drinking. Laughing out loud. Turning your body right away from the qibla, or deciding to stop. If one of these happens, put it right and pray it again from the beginning. But read the rest of this page first, because almost every one of them has an exception, and most of what a beginner worries about is on the other list.

Where it appears: What breaks the prayer — What actually breaks it?
English: Smiling is not laughing, and nobody has ever held that it breaks a prayer. What is meant is laughing aloud.

Where it appears: What breaks the prayer — What actually breaks it?
English: Ibn al-Mundhir recorded the scholars as agreed that laughing aloud ends the prayer, and an-Nawawi and Ibn Qudamah both record that most of them held smiling does not. It is one of the few things on this page nobody argues about. One thing they do differ on is what else it costs you: the Maliki, Shafi`i and Hanbali schools hold that laughing aloud ends the prayer but leaves your wudu intact, so you stand up and pray again. The Hanafi school holds that it ends the wudu too, so someone following that school washes first. If you are not sure which applies to you, washing again costs a minute.

Where it appears: What breaks the prayer — What if I am facing the wrong way?
English: What if I am facing the wrong way?

Where it appears: What breaks the prayer — What if I am facing the wrong way?
English: This one is narrower than it sounds. What ends the prayer is turning your whole body away from the qibla with no reason to. Getting the direction wrong, in a hotel room or on a plane or in a city you do not know, does not, as long as you worked it out as best you could. If you find out afterwards that you were off, the prayer stands.

Where it appears: What breaks the prayer — What if I am facing the wrong way?
English: A whole congregation once turned right around in the middle of Fajr, and their prayer counted.

Where it appears: What breaks the prayer — What if I am facing the wrong way?
English: The people of Quba were praying facing Jerusalem when someone arrived to say the direction had been changed to the Ka`bah that night, so they turned mid-prayer and carried on. Bukhari puts the narration under a chapter heading that includes those who held there is no need to repeat a prayer offered by mistake in the wrong direction.

Where it appears: What breaks the prayer — What if I speak without thinking?
English: What if I speak without thinking?

Where it appears: What breaks the prayer — What if I speak without thinking?
English: A companion said "Allah have mercy on you" to a man who sneezed mid-prayer, not knowing he could not. Afterwards the Prophet ﷺ taught him, without scolding him and by his own account better than anyone had ever taught him anything, that this prayer is not the place for ordinary speech. He was not told to pray it again. Deliberate speech ends the prayer; speech before you knew the rule, or in a moment of forgetfulness, does not.

Where it appears: What breaks the prayer — What if I speak without thinking?
English: This was not always the rule. People used to speak to each other in prayer and were told to stop, which is why the narrations about it read the way they do.

Where it appears: What breaks the prayer — What if I speak without thinking?
English: Zayd ibn Arqam: "we used to speak while praying, and one of us would tell his companion what he needed, until the verse was revealed and we were ordered to be silent." Ibn Mas`ud used to greet the Prophet ﷺ mid-prayer and be answered, and returned from Abyssinia to find that he was not: "there is occupation enough in the prayer".

Where it appears: What breaks the prayer — What if I think I broke wudu?
English: What if I think I broke wudu?

Where it appears: What breaks the prayer — What if I think I broke wudu?
English: Doubt does not. Someone asked the Prophet ﷺ about feeling as though they had passed wind mid-prayer, and he said not to leave the prayer unless they heard a sound or smelled something. Uncertainty is not enough. Carry on.
Français: Le doute, non. Quelqu’un a interrogé le Prophète ﷺ sur l’impression d’avoir rompu son wudu en pleine prière, et il a répondu de ne pas quitter la prière à moins d’entendre un son ou de sentir une odeur. L’incertitude ne suffit pas. Continuez.
Español: La duda no. Alguien preguntó al Profeta ﷺ sobre la sensación de haber expulsado gases en plena oración, y dijo que no dejara la oración a menos que oyera un sonido u oliera algo. La incertidumbre no basta. Sigue.

Where it appears: What breaks the prayer — What if I think I broke wudu?
English: This is the hadith to remember if you find yourself checking constantly. The rule is deliberately strict about certainty, because doubt would otherwise end every prayer.
Français: C’est le hadith à retenir si vous vous surprenez à vérifier sans cesse. La règle est volontairement stricte sur la certitude, car le doute mettrait sinon fin à chaque prière.
Español: Este es el hadiz que recordar si te encuentras comprobándolo constantemente. La regla es deliberadamente estricta con la certeza, porque de otro modo la duda acabaría con cada oración.

Where it appears: What is Islam? — Is it belief, or practice?
English: Is it belief, or practice?

Where it appears: What is Islam? — Is it belief, or practice?
English: When the angel Jibril asked the Prophet ﷺ about this in front of his companions, the answer came in two parts: what you believe, and what you do. Neither stands alone. That is why this app teaches the prayer and the belief side by side rather than one first and one later.
Français: Quand l’ange Jibril interrogea le Prophète ﷺ à ce sujet devant ses compagnons, la réponse vint en deux parties : ce que l’on croit, et ce que l’on fait. Ni l’une ni l’autre ne tient seule. C’est pourquoi cette application enseigne la prière et la croyance côte à côte, plutôt que l’une d’abord et l’autre ensuite.
Español: Cuando el ángel Yibril preguntó al Profeta ﷺ sobre esto delante de sus compañeros, la respuesta llegó en dos partes: lo que crees y lo que haces. Ninguna se sostiene sola. Por eso esta aplicación enseña la oración y la creencia a la vez, en lugar de una primero y otra después.

Where it appears: What is Islam? — Is it meant to be this hard?
English: Is it meant to be this hard?

Where it appears: What is Islam? — Is it meant to be this hard?
English: You are not behind. The Prophet ﷺ said the religion is easy, and that whoever overburdens themselves in it will not keep it up, so take the next thing rather than all of it. The Qur’an says God does not ask of anyone more than they can bear.

Where it appears: What is Islam? — What does it ask of me?
English: What does it ask of me?

Where it appears: What is Islam? — What does it ask of me?
English: The testimony of faith, the five daily prayers, zakat, a yearly share of savings given to those entitled to it, fasting in Ramadan, and the pilgrimage to Mecca once in a lifetime for anyone able to make it. The Prophet ﷺ described Islam as built on these five.

Where it appears: What is Islam? — What does the word mean?
English: What does the word mean?

Where it appears: What is Islam? — What does the word mean?
English: Islam is an Arabic word meaning submission, giving yourself over to God. A Muslim is someone who does that. It comes from the same root as salam, peace, and the two ideas sit together: peace through no longer being pulled in every direction at once.

Where it appears: What is Islam? — What is at the centre of it?
English: What is at the centre of it?

Where it appears: What is Islam? — What is at the centre of it?
English: Everything else rests on this. Islam teaches that there is one God, Allah, the Arabic word for God used by Arabic-speaking Christians and Jews too, and that worship belongs to Him alone, with nothing and no one sharing it. Saying and meaning that is what makes a person Muslim.

Where it appears: What is Islam? — What is at the centre of it?
English: Nobody can be forced into this. The Qur’an says plainly that there is no compulsion in religion.
Français: Nul ne peut y être contraint. Le Coran dit clairement qu’il n’y a pas de contrainte en religion.
Español: Nadie puede ser forzado a esto. El Corán dice con claridad que no hay coacción en la religión.

Where it appears: What is the Qur’an? — Am I already reading it?
English: Am I already reading it?

Where it appears: What is the Qur’an? — Am I already reading it?
English: The Qur’an is not only read, it is recited, in every prayer, out loud or quietly. Al-Fatihah, its opening chapter of seven short verses, is said in every unit of every prayer for the rest of your life. Learning it is the single most useful thing a new Muslim can memorise.

Where it appears: What is the Qur’an? — Am I already reading it?
English: Until you know it, say what you can and keep learning. Nobody starts fluent, and the Practice screen exists to take it a line at a time.
Français: En attendant de la savoir, dites ce que vous pouvez et continuez d’apprendre. Personne ne commence à l’aise, et l’écran de pratique existe pour l’aborder ligne par ligne.
Español: Hasta que la sepas, di lo que puedas y sigue aprendiendo. Nadie empieza con soltura, y la pantalla de práctica existe para tomarla línea a línea.

Where it appears: What is the Qur’an? — What do Muslims believe it is?
English: What do Muslims believe it is?

Where it appears: What is the Qur’an? — What do Muslims believe it is?
English: Not a book about God, but the speech of God, revealed in Arabic to Muhammad ﷺ through the angel Jibril over about twenty-three years, and preserved unchanged since. That is the claim, and it is why the Arabic itself matters so much: a translation is understood as an explanation of the Qur’an rather than the Qur’an.

Where it appears: What is the Qur’an? — Where should I start?
English: Where should I start?

Where it appears: What is the Qur’an? — Where should I start?
English: Start small and start with sound. Learn Al-Fatihah, then a few of the short chapters at the end, listening and repeating rather than reading silently. The Prophet ﷺ said the best of people are those who learn the Qur’an and teach it. Learning it is the point, and it is slow for everyone.

Where it appears: What is the Qur’an? — Why does it not start at the beginning?
English: Why does it not start at the beginning?

Where it appears: What is the Qur’an? — Why does it not start at the beginning?
English: It has 114 chapters, called surahs, made of verses called ayahs. They are not in the order they were revealed, and it is not a story told front to back, so reading it cover to cover like a novel is not how most people start, and struggling with that is not a failure of yours.

Where it appears: What is the Sunnah? — Are all hadith reliable?
English: Are all hadith reliable?

Where it appears: What is the Sunnah? — Are all hadith reliable?
English: Because hadith were transmitted by people, scholars spent centuries grading them, examining every chain and every narrator. Some are sound, some are weak, and some are forgeries. This is why the app names its sources: so you can check, rather than take its word.

Where it appears: What is the Sunnah? — Are all hadith reliable?
English: Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim are the two collections Sunni scholars regard as the most rigorously authenticated. Other collections contain both strong and weak reports, which is why a grading matters there and not in these two.
Français: Sahih al-Bukhari et Sahih Muslim sont les deux recueils que les savants sunnites tiennent pour les plus rigoureusement authentifiés. D’autres recueils contiennent des rapports forts et faibles, et c’est pourquoi la classification y compte, alors qu’elle ne s’impose pas dans ces deux-là.
Español: Sahih al-Bujari y Sahih Muslim son las dos colecciones que los sabios sunníes consideran las más rigurosamente autentificadas. Otras colecciones contienen relatos fuertes y débiles, y por eso allí importa la clasificación y en estas dos no.

Where it appears: What is the Sunnah? — What does it look like day to day?
English: What does it look like day to day?

Where it appears: What is the Sunnah? — What does it look like day to day?
English: Much of it is small and human: not harming a neighbour, making a guest welcome, saying something good or staying quiet, eating with the right hand, a few words before sleeping. Following the Sunnah is not an extra layer of difficulty on top of the religion. A lot of it is simply how a decent person moves through a day.

Where it appears: What is the Sunnah? — What does Sunnah mean?
English: What does Sunnah mean?

Where it appears: What is the Sunnah? — What does Sunnah mean?
English: Sunnah means a way or a path, and specifically the way the Prophet ﷺ lived: what he said, what he did, and what he approved of in others. It reaches us through hadith, which are reports of those things recorded with the chain of people who passed each one down.

Where it appears: What is the Sunnah? — Why does it sit beside the Qur’an?
English: Why does it sit beside the Qur’an?

Where it appears: What is the Sunnah? — Why does it sit beside the Qur’an?
English: The Qur’an gives the command and the Sunnah usually gives the method. "Establish the prayer" appears again and again; how many units, when, and what to say in them comes from watching him. The Qur’an itself instructs Muslims to take what the Messenger gives them.
Français: Le Coran donne l’ordre et la Sunna donne généralement la méthode. « Accomplissez la prière » revient sans cesse ; combien d’unités, à quel moment et que dire dedans vient de l’avoir observé. Le Coran lui-même ordonne aux musulmans de prendre ce que le Messager leur donne.
Español: El Corán da la orden y la Sunna suele dar el método. «Estableced la oración» aparece una y otra vez; cuántas unidades, cuándo y qué decir en ellas viene de observarlo a él. El propio Corán instruye a los musulmanes a tomar lo que el Mensajero les da.

Where it appears: What you need before you pray — Am I covered, and is the place clean?
English: Am I covered, and is the place clean?

Where it appears: What you need before you pray — Am I covered, and is the place clean?
English: The Qur’an tells people to take their adornment at every place of prayer, so dress as you would to meet someone you respect. Your clothes and the ground you pray on should be clean. A carpet, a towel or a mat is fine; a prayer mat is convenient, not required.

Where it appears: What you need before you pray — Am I covered, and is the place clean?
English: How much has to be covered differs a little between men and women and is set out in the clothing guide. Ordinary loose clothes cover it for most people.
Français: La surface à couvrir diffère un peu entre les hommes et les femmes et figure dans le guide sur les vêtements. Des vêtements amples ordinaires suffisent pour la plupart des gens.
Español: Cuánto hay que cubrir varía un poco entre hombres y mujeres y está explicado en la guía de ropa. La ropa holgada corriente lo cubre para la mayoría.

Where it appears: What you need before you pray — Am I in wudu?
English: Am I in wudu?

Where it appears: What you need before you pray — Am I in wudu?
English: Wudu is the short wash before prayer. The Prophet ﷺ said the prayer of someone who has broken it is not accepted until they wash again. One wudu covers several prayers. It lasts until something breaks it, and the wudu guide sets out what does and what only feels as though it does.

Where it appears: What you need before you pray — Do I have to say the intention?
English: Do I have to say the intention?

Where it appears: What you need before you pray — Do I have to say the intention?
English: The intention is a thought, not a sentence: knowing which prayer you are about to pray. You do not say it out loud, and you do not need a formula. If you are standing on a mat about to pray Maghrib, you have already intended it.
Français: L’intention est une pensée, non une phrase : savoir quelle prière vous allez faire. On ne la dit pas à voix haute et aucune formule n’est requise. Si vous êtes debout sur une natte pour prier le Maghrib, vous en avez déjà formé l’intention.
Español: La intención es un pensamiento, no una frase: saber qué oración estás a punto de hacer. No se dice en voz alta y no hace falta una fórmula. Si estás de pie sobre una esterilla a punto de rezar el Magrib, ya la has intentado.

Where it appears: What you need before you pray — Do I have to say the intention?
English: Some people are taught to say the intention aloud. Scholars differ on whether that is recommended, and nobody holds that the prayer fails without it.
Français: On enseigne à certains de dire l’intention à voix haute. Les savants divergent sur son caractère recommandé, et aucun ne soutient que la prière échoue sans cela.
Español: A algunas personas se les enseña a decir la intención en voz alta. Los sabios difieren sobre si eso es recomendable, y ninguno sostiene que la oración falle sin ello.

Where it appears: What you need before you pray — Do I have to say the intention?
English: Most of this is agreed and only one part of it is open. The imams agree that the place of the intention is the heart and that the prayer never asks you to speak it, so that is not one side of an argument. What they differ on is whether voicing it is recommended. Ibn Taymiyyah, who records both views, reports that scholars among the followers of Abu Hanifah, ash-Shafi`i and Ahmad held it recommended as a way of making the intention firmer, and that scholars among the followers of Malik and Ahmad held it is not, because neither the Prophet ﷺ nor his Companions did it; he takes the second view. This note used to give the first row as the majority and the second as a minority, which counted scholars nobody has counted and put an agreed point on one side of a disagreement. If you were taught to say it, saying it harms nothing.

Where it appears: What you need before you pray — Do I have to say the intention?
English: Scholars of the school held that voicing the intention is recommended, as a way of making it firmer. The same view is found among Shafi`i and Hanbali scholars.

Where it appears: What you need before you pray — Do I have to say the intention?
English: Scholars of the school held that voicing it is not recommended, since neither the Prophet ﷺ nor his Companions did it. The same view is found among Hanbali scholars.

Where it appears: What you need before you pray — Is it the right time?
English: Is it the right time?

Where it appears: What you need before you pray — Is it the right time?
English: Each prayer has a window, and you pray inside it rather than whenever you like, and the Qur’an calls prayer a decree of specified times. The Pray tab works the times out from where you are, on the phone, so you do not have to calculate anything.

Where it appears: What you need before you pray — Is it the right time?
English: If your local mosque prints a timetable and it differs from the app by a few minutes, follow the mosque.

Where it appears: What you need before you pray — Is it the right time?
English: The app works the times out from the position of the sun, which is arithmetic. A mosque timetable is a decision: which twilight angle to use for Fajr and Isha, whether to round to the nearest five minutes, whether to hold Isha back in summer so people can get there. Both are honest answers to the same question and they land a few minutes apart. Praying with the congregation you actually pray with matters more than the arithmetic, and the differences are almost always small enough that either time falls inside the window anyway. The one place it is worth checking is high summer in a northern country, where Fajr and Isha can crowd together and mosques handle it in noticeably different ways.

Where it appears: What you need before you pray — Which way do I face?
English: Which way do I face?

Where it appears: What you need before you pray — Which way do I face?
English: Muslims face the Kaʿbah in Mecca, and the Qur’an gives that instruction directly. The Qibla screen in this app points the way from where you are. If you cannot work it out, on a plane or in an unfamiliar place, face your best guess and pray; that is accepted.

Where it appears: When you get it wrong — How is it received?
English: How is it received?

Where it appears: When you get it wrong — How is it received?
English: The Prophet ﷺ described God as more pleased with a person’s repentance than someone would be who lost their camel in the desert and then found it. The image is not of a grudging pardon. It is relief and delight.
Français: Le Prophète ﷺ a décrit Dieu comme plus heureux du repentir d’une personne que ne le serait quelqu’un qui a perdu son chameau dans le désert et l’a retrouvé. L’image n’est pas celle d’un pardon consenti à contrecœur. C’est le soulagement et la joie.
Español: El Profeta ﷺ describió a Dios como más complacido con el arrepentimiento de una persona que alguien que perdió su camello en el desierto y luego lo encontró. La imagen no es de un perdón a regañadientes. Es alivio y alegría.

Where it appears: When you get it wrong — Is it too late for me?
English: Is it too late for me?

Where it appears: When you get it wrong — Is it too late for me?
English: The Qur’an addresses people who have wronged themselves and tells them not to despair of God’s mercy, because He forgives all sins. That verse is worth knowing early, because the thing most likely to end someone’s practice is not a sin. It is deciding afterwards that they are past helping.

Where it appears: When you get it wrong — What does repentance actually take?
English: What does repentance actually take?

Where it appears: When you get it wrong — What does repentance actually take?
English: Stopping, meaning it, and asking. There is no ritual, no witness, and nobody to confess to. You turn to God directly. The Qur’an calls it turning to Him with sincere repentance, and that is the whole procedure.

Where it appears: When you get it wrong — What if I do it again?
English: What if I do it again?

Where it appears: When you get it wrong — What if I do it again?
English: You repent again. People expect to fail once and be finished; that is not how it works, and a habit that takes a year to break took a year for everybody else too. Keep praying while you work on it. Stopping the prayer because you feel unworthy of it is the one move that makes things worse.

Where it appears: When you get it wrong — What if I do it again?
English: Nobody is owed an account of your sins. You do not have to tell an imam, a friend, or anyone at the mosque.
Français: Personne n’a droit au récit de vos fautes. Vous n’avez à en parler ni à un imam, ni à un ami, ni à personne à la mosquée.
Español: A nadie se le debe un relato de tus faltas. No tienes que contárselo a un imán, a un amigo ni a nadie de la mezquita.

Where it appears: Who is Allah? — How do I get to know Him?
English: How do I get to know Him?

Where it appears: Who is Allah? — How do I get to know Him?
English: Through His names, rather than in the abstract, and you will meet them constantly.

Where it appears: Who is Allah? — How do I get to know Him?
English: Learning a few is a gentler way in than trying to think about God in the abstract.

Where it appears: Who is Allah? — Is Allah a different God?
English: Is Allah a different God?

Where it appears: Who is Allah? — Is Allah a different God?
English: No. Allah is simply the Arabic word for God, and Arabic-speaking Christians and Jews use it when they pray.

Where it appears: Who is Allah? — Is Allah a different God?
English: It has no plural and no gender, which is part of why Muslims keep the word rather than translating it.

Where it appears: Who is Allah? — What if I try to picture Him?
English: What if I try to picture Him?

Where it appears: Who is Allah? — What if I try to picture Him?
English: Any picture you form is wrong by definition, and you are not expected to form one.

Where it appears: Who is Allah? — What if I try to picture Him?
English: This is why Muslims do not depict God, and why you will not find images of Him anywhere in Islam.

Where it appears: Who is Allah? — What was said when the Prophet ﷺ was asked to describe God?
English: What was said when the Prophet ﷺ was asked to describe God?

Where it appears: Who is Allah? — What was said when the Prophet ﷺ was asked to describe God?
English: A short chapter of the Qur’an, and Muslims have taken it as the definition ever since.

Where it appears: Who is Muhammad ﷺ? — Do Muslims worship him?
English: Do Muslims worship him?

Where it appears: Who is Muhammad ﷺ? — Do Muslims worship him?
English: Muhammad ﷺ was born in Mecca around 570 CE and received the Qur’an over roughly twenty-three years. Muslims believe he is the last of a long line of prophets that includes Ibrahim, Musa and ʿIsa, or Abraham, Moses and Jesus. He is not divine and is not worshipped. He delivered the message; the message is from God.

Where it appears: Who is Muhammad ﷺ? — What is the ﷺ after his name?
English: What is the ﷺ after his name?

Where it appears: Who is Muhammad ﷺ? — What is the ﷺ after his name?
English: You will see ﷺ written after his name throughout this app and everywhere else. It stands for an Arabic phrase asking God to bless him and grant him peace. Muslims say it aloud out of respect whenever he is mentioned. Nobody will mind if you forget at first.
Français: Vous verrez ﷺ écrit après son nom dans toute cette application et partout ailleurs. Cela représente une formule arabe demandant à Dieu de le bénir et de lui accorder la paix. Les musulmans la prononcent par respect chaque fois qu’il est mentionné. Personne ne vous en voudra si vous l’oubliez au début.
Español: Verás ﷺ escrito tras su nombre en toda esta aplicación y en todas partes. Representa una frase árabe que pide a Dios que lo bendiga y le conceda la paz. Los musulmanes la dicen en voz alta por respeto cada vez que se le menciona. A nadie le importará si al principio se te olvida.

Where it appears: Who is Muhammad ﷺ? — What was he like?
English: What was he like?

Where it appears: Who is Muhammad ﷺ? — What was he like?
English: The Qur’an describes him as being of great character, and the people who lived with him described someone who never used foul or crude language and who taught that the best people are those with the best manners. Much of what Muslims try to imitate is not ritual at all. It is how he treated people.

Where it appears: Who is Muhammad ﷺ? — Why follow him?
English: Why follow him?

Where it appears: Who is Muhammad ﷺ? — Why follow him?
English: Because the Qur’an tells them to. It calls him an excellent example, and says that obeying him is obeying God. In practice this is very concrete: the Qur’an commands prayer without describing how, and the answer to "how" is that he said, "Pray as you have seen me praying."
Français: Parce que le Coran le leur dit. Il l’appelle un excellent modèle et dit que lui obéir, c’est obéir à Dieu. En pratique, c’est très concret : le Coran ordonne la prière sans en décrire la forme, et la réponse au « comment » est qu’il a dit : « Priez comme vous m’avez vu prier ».
Español: Porque el Corán se lo dice. Lo llama un excelente ejemplo y dice que obedecerle es obedecer a Dios. En la práctica esto es muy concreto: el Corán ordena la oración sin describir cómo, y la respuesta al «cómo» es que él dijo: «Orad como me habéis visto orar».

Where it appears: Who is Muhammad ﷺ? — Why follow him?
English: Loving and following him is not the same as worshipping him. The distinction matters to Muslims and is worth being clear about early.
Français: L’aimer et le suivre n’est pas la même chose que l’adorer. La distinction compte pour les musulmans et il vaut mieux la clarifier tôt.
Español: Amarlo y seguirlo no es lo mismo que adorarlo. La distinción importa a los musulmanes y conviene tenerla clara pronto.

Where it appears: Witr — Face the qibla and intend
English: Stand facing the qibla, feet roughly shoulder-width apart, and intend in your heart that you are praying Witr.

Where it appears: Witr — Is one really enough?
English: Is one really enough?

Where it appears: Witr — Is one really enough?
English: Yes. The Prophet ﷺ named five, three and one, and left the choice to the person praying, so one is a complete witr rather than a shortened version of something else. Most people pray three, and you will see that around you.

Where it appears: Witr — Is one really enough?
English: Start with one. It is the whole prayer, it takes a minute, and it is the version you are least likely to get wrong while you are learning.

Where it appears: Witr — Turn to your left
English: That is Witr complete.

Where it appears: Witr — What if I sleep through it?
English: What if I sleep through it?

Where it appears: Witr — What if I sleep through it?
English: Pray it before you go to bed. Leaving it to the end of the night is better, but only if you are actually going to be awake. It is meant to be the last thing you pray, not the thing you missed.

Where it appears: Witr — Why an odd number?
English: Why an odd number?

Where it appears: Witr — Why an odd number?
English: Because that is what the word means, and it is what you finish the night on.

Where it appears: Work and money — How does Islam see work?
English: How does Islam see work?

Where it appears: Work and money — How does Islam see work?
English: There is no ideal of poverty here. The Prophet ﷺ said nobody has eaten better food than what he earned by his own hands, and noted that the Prophet Dawud ate from his own labour. The Qur’an tells people to disperse and seek God’s bounty as soon as the Friday prayer ends.
Français: Il n’y a pas ici d’idéal de pauvreté. Le Prophète ﷺ a dit que personne n’a mangé meilleure nourriture que celle gagnée de ses propres mains, et a rappelé que le prophète Dawud mangeait du fruit de son travail. Le Coran dit aux gens de se disperser et de rechercher la faveur de Dieu dès que la prière du vendredi s’achève.
Español: Aquí no hay un ideal de pobreza. El Profeta ﷺ dijo que nadie ha comido mejor alimento que el que ganó con sus propias manos, y señaló que el profeta Dawud comía de su propio trabajo. El Corán dice a la gente que se disperse y busque el favor de Dios en cuanto termina la oración del viernes.

Where it appears: Work and money — What about interest?
English: What about interest?

Where it appears: Work and money — What about interest?
English: Riba, usually translated as interest or usury, is prohibited in the Qur’an in strong terms, and the Prophet ﷺ listed consuming it among the gravest sins. In practice this is what makes conventional mortgages, interest-bearing savings and most credit cards a live question for Muslims.

Where it appears: Work and money — What about interest?
English: If you already have a mortgage or a loan, you have not ruined anything and you do not have to solve it this month. Islamic finance options exist in many countries and vary a great deal. Scholars have discussed this in more detail, so get advice on your actual situation.

Where it appears: Work and money — What if my job touches something forbidden?
English: What if my job touches something forbidden?

Where it appears: Work and money — What if my job touches something forbidden?
English: Directly producing or selling what is prohibited is the clear case. The Prophet ﷺ said the curse on wine falls on ten, its seller and the one who lives off its price among them. What is less clear is indirect involvement: a supermarket cashier who occasionally scans wine, a delivery driver, an accountant at a bank. That distance is exactly what scholars weigh.

Where it appears: Work and money — What if my job touches something forbidden?
English: Scholars differ on how much distance from a prohibited thing is enough, so answers vary by how central it is to the job.
Français: Les savants divergent sur la distance suffisante par rapport à une chose interdite, si bien que les réponses varient selon la place qu’elle occupe dans le travail.
Español: Los sabios difieren sobre cuánta distancia de lo prohibido basta, así que las respuestas varían según lo central que sea en el trabajo.

Where it appears: Work and money — What if my job touches something forbidden?
English: The usual reasoning looks at whether the forbidden thing is the point of the work or incidental to it, at how much of your income depends on it, and at what leaving would cost you. Someone whose whole income is from selling alcohol is in a different position from someone who occasionally rings it through a till, and someone who cannot simply leave is in a different position again. This note used to set out two positions and attribute one to the majority and one to contemporary scholarship, which stated a count nobody has taken, and the first of them was not a disagreement at all, since the clear case is agreed. Where scholars actually differ is on the line, and the line moves with the facts, which is why the answer here is to describe your actual job to someone qualified rather than to read a general rule off a page.

Where it appears: Work and money — What if my job touches something forbidden?
English: Do not quit your job the week you become Muslim. Find out what your options are first.
Français: Ne quittez pas votre emploi la semaine où vous devenez musulman. Renseignez-vous d’abord sur vos options.
Español: No dejes tu trabajo la semana en que te haces musulmán. Averigua primero qué opciones tienes.

Where it appears: Wudu — Finish
English: Finish

Where it appears: Wudu — Finish
English: When you are done, say:

Where it appears: Wudu — Finish
English: You are now ready to pray.

Where it appears: Wudu — Finish
English: If you are ever rushed or short of water, the four parts the Qur’an itself names are the face, the arms to the elbows, wiping the head, and the feet to the ankles. Once each is enough. Everything else here is the fuller way the Prophet ﷺ did it.

Where it appears: Wudu — Finish
English: Schools differ over what else is strictly required beyond those four. The intention, keeping to the order, and washing without long pauses in between are each treated as a requirement in some schools and as a recommendation in others. Teaching the full method sidesteps the question entirely, which is why this guide does. Knowing the shorter version matters on the day you have half a bottle of water and a prayer to catch.

Where it appears: Wudu — Intend
English: Intend in your heart that you are performing wudu to purify yourself for prayer, then say:

Where it appears: Wudu — Intend
English: One wudu covers as many prayers as you like. It lasts until something breaks it, and only then do you wash again.

Where it appears: Wudu — Intend
English: What certainly breaks it: anything that leaves you from the front or the back, such as using the toilet or passing wind, and losing awareness, whether through sleep deep enough that you would not have noticed, fainting, or anything else that takes your senses away.

Where it appears: Wudu — Intend
English: Bukhari 135 is the Prophet's ﷺ words that the prayer of someone who breaks their wudu is not accepted until they wash again. Abu Huraira, asked what breaking it meant, answered: passing wind. On sleep the wording is "the eyes are the drawstring of the backside, so whoever sleeps should perform wudu". Schools qualify that by how deeply and in what position, but all four agree that heavy sleep ends it, and all four agree that losing your senses another way, whether fainting, anaesthetic or being drunk, ends it too, which is why this note names that rather than only sleep.

Where it appears: Wudu — Intend
English: Two more are handled differently by the schools: touching your own private parts, and skin contact with the opposite sex. If one of those happens and you are unsure, washing again takes a minute and settles it.

Where it appears: Wudu — Intend
English: The split is not carelessness. It is two authentic narrations pointing different ways. Busrah bint Safwan reports "whoever touches his penis should not pray until he performs wudu"; Talq ibn `Ali reports the Prophet ﷺ answering "is it anything other than a piece of him?" Tirmidhi grades both sound and records that the second is the position of the scholars of Kufa. On the opposite sex, the verse says "or you have touched women", and the argument is over whether that word means intercourse or ordinary contact; `A'isha reports that the Prophet ﷺ kissed her and prayed without washing again.

Where it appears: Wudu — Intend
English: Neither of the two breaks wudu on its own.

Where it appears: Wudu — Intend
English: Both break it where there is desire: the private parts touched deliberately with the palm, and contact with the opposite sex accompanied by desire.

Where it appears: Wudu — Intend
English: Both break it regardless of intention: the private parts touched with the palm and no barrier, and skin contact with an adult of the opposite sex who is not a close relative.

Where it appears: Wudu — Intend
English: Touching the private parts breaks it; contact with the opposite sex breaks it where there is desire.

Where it appears: Wudu — Intend; Ghusl — Intend; Tayammum — Intend
English: Intend

Where it appears: Wudu — Rinse your mouth
English: Rinse your mouth

Where it appears: Wudu — Rinse your mouth
English: Take water into your mouth with your right hand, swill it around and spit it out. Three times.

Where it appears: Wudu — Rinse your nose
English: Rinse your nose

Where it appears: Wudu — Rinse your nose
English: Sniff a little water into your nose with your right hand, then blow it out using your left. Three times.

Where it appears: Wudu — Rinse your nose
English: Draw it up properly, unless you are fasting, in which case go gently.

Where it appears: Wudu — Wash your arms
English: Wash your arms

Where it appears: Wudu — Wash your arms
English: Wash your right arm from the fingertips to just past the elbow, three times. Then the left, three times.

Where it appears: Wudu — Wash your arms
English: Right before left is the pattern for everything that comes in a pair.

Where it appears: Wudu — Wash your face
English: Wash your face

Where it appears: Wudu — Wash your face
English: Wash your whole face three times, from your hairline to under your chin and from ear to ear.

Where it appears: Wudu — Wash your feet
English: Wash your right foot to just past the ankle, between the toes, three times. Then the left, three times.

Where it appears: Wudu — Wash your feet; Ghusl — Wash your feet
English: Wash your feet

Where it appears: Wudu — Wash your hands
English: Wash both hands up to the wrists, three times, between the fingers.

Where it appears: Wudu — Wash your hands; Ghusl — Wash your hands
English: Wash your hands

Where it appears: Wudu — Wipe your ears
English: Wipe your ears

Where it appears: Wudu — Wipe your ears
English: With the same wetness, put your index fingers inside your ears and your thumbs behind them, and wipe. Once.

Where it appears: Wudu — Wipe your head
English: Wipe your head

Where it appears: Wudu — Wipe your head
English: With wet hands, wipe over your head from the front to the back and return to the front. Once.

Where it appears: Wudu — Wipe your head
English: Wiping, not washing, and once rather than three times.

Where it appears: Your first time at a mosque — What do I do when I walk in?
English: What do I do when I walk in?

Where it appears: Your first time at a mosque — What do I do when I walk in?
English: There will be a shoe rack by the door. Take your shoes off there and carry them in if the rack is full. Step in with your right foot. There are usually separate entrances or areas for men and women. Look for the signs, or ask; nobody minds being asked.

Where it appears: Your first time at a mosque — What happens afterwards?
English: What happens afterwards?

Where it appears: Your first time at a mosque — What happens afterwards?
English: People turn and greet whoever is beside them. Say salam back. Someone will very likely ask if you are new. This is the moment the whole trip is actually for, and it is worth staying ten minutes for it.

Where it appears: Your first time at a mosque — What happens in the prayer?
English: What happens in the prayer?

Where it appears: Your first time at a mosque — What happens in the prayer?
English: People stand shoulder to shoulder in straight lines, filling from the front. Stand in a line, follow the imam, and do what the row does. You do not say anything aloud and nobody is watching you.

Where it appears: Your first time at a mosque — What if I get something wrong?
English: What if I get something wrong?

Where it appears: Your first time at a mosque — What if I get something wrong?
English: Being a beat behind in the movements. Not knowing where to stand. Your phone going off. Asking a stranger what to do. Leaving straight after. Getting the words wrong under your breath.

Where it appears: Your first time at a mosque — What if I get something wrong?
English: Everyone in that room was new once, including the imam. Nobody is grading you, and the ones who notice you are new are almost always pleased about it.

Where it appears: Your first time at a mosque — What should I do before I go?
English: What should I do before I go?

Where it appears: Your first time at a mosque — What should I do before I go?
English: Do your wudu at home if you can. It is one less thing to work out when you arrive. Wear clean clothes that cover you from the navel to the knees at minimum; loose trousers and a long top are entirely normal. What a woman covers is no different here from anywhere else in front of men outside the family, and the clothing guide sets it out with the verses behind it.

English: When should I go the first time?

Where it appears: Your first time at a mosque — When should I go the first time?
English: Friday midday is the busiest hour of the week. For a first visit, go for a normal prayer: Dhuhr in the early afternoon, or ʿIshaʾ at night. Fewer people, more room to watch what everyone else does.

Where it appears: Your first time at a mosque — When should I go the first time?
English: Friday prayer is obligatory for men, so you will need to go eventually. It is easier once the building is already familiar.

English: Where do I sit?

Where it appears: Your first time at a mosque — Where do I sit?
English: Pray two short rakʿah before you sit down. It is what everyone does on entering. Then sit anywhere on the carpet. There is no reserved seating and no collection.

Where it appears: Your first time at a mosque — Where do I sit?
English: If a prayer is already in progress, join the line where you are and follow along from wherever the imam has got to.
